summary: Ohio's Lorain West Breakwater light: an 1830s pier light's successor, a 1917 concrete tower lit in 1919, closed in 1966 and restored by volunteers.

lens.where: Lorain Port Authority offices, Black River Landing (2014)

structures.note: Black River light-station tower at the end of the west pier; rebuilt of brick 1857, replaced 1875.
46-foot wooden square pyramidal tower at the end of a 600-foot extension (1875).

Rear range tower on the west pier, erected by contract after the 1891 appropriation; blown off its temporary foundation on 21 February 1912 and discontinued once the acetylene breakwater light was established.
Keepers' tower with lantern; permanent light 7 April 1919.

access.note: Open only through the Lorain Lighthouse Foundation's seasonal tours and sunset dinners, reached by boat; closed for the winter of 2026 (Foundation home page).

visit.note: Reached by boat; tours from June to the autumn.

facts.agency: Lorain Lighthouse Foundation (operator); Port of Lorain Foundation owned the building from 1990 per the library

events.note: Congress appropriates $2,600 to establish and build the Black River light-station.
Cylindrical brick tower with a lantern room, lit by eight lard-oil lamps (Black River light-station).
Tower rebuilt of brick and fitted with a fourth-order Fresnel lens.
Brick tower torn down; a 46-foot wooden tower lit 18 September 1875 at the end of a new 600-foot pier extension.
Congress appropriates money for a shore-side rear range tower; a skeleton iron tower is erected by contract.
Rear range light first exhibited from the skeletal iron tower on 15 October 1893.
Schooner Alta strikes the rear tower and the tower falls, shattering three lens lanterns; date disputed (16 Aug per the library; 22 June per LighthouseFriends).
Two Lorain Harbor lights changed from fixed to flashing; illuminant changed from oil to acetylene.
21 February 1912: high winds blow the rear range tower off its temporary foundation.
Act of 22 October 1913 appropriates $35,000 for a light and fog-signal station at Lorain Harbor.
Concrete structure erected by 30 June 1917; temporary light in the new lantern.
Permanent fourth-order light placed in commission on 7 April 1919.
Diaphone fog signal placed in commission 13 May 1919.
Wooden tower at the end of the west pier replaced by a skeletal steel tower on commercial power; a double keepers' dwelling on Augusta Avenue transferred to the Service.
The Coast Guard takes control of U.S. lighthouses.
Harbor improvements plan an automated tower at the western tip of the outer breakwall; the Coast Guard plans to demolish the old light.
Coast Guard decommissions the lighthouse; last light shown 10 January 1966.
25 January 1966: five-year lease to a not-for-profit association; demolition contract cancelled.
Canadian freighter accidentally rams the lighthouse.
Coast Guard returns the building to the General Services Administration as surplus.
Deed to the Lorain County Historical Society for one dollar, on condition it be kept as a historic landmark.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places (NPGallery date 29 December 1978).
Port of Lorain Foundation buys the building for one dollar.
Army Corps of Engineers stabilizes the base by grouting; cost about $850,000.
A navigational light re-established in the lantern room after 35 years of darkness (2001-2002).
First year visitors are taken on tours of the building.
Fourth-order lens returns to Lorain on loan from the Coast Guard, until 1 September 2028.
Fourth-order lens placed on display at the Port Authority offices, Black River Landing.
Ohio Historical Marker dedicated at the 2017 centennial.

corrections.why: The record's station point is about 0.6 km from the tower coordinates the record also lists (41.477572, -82.190559), and from the USLHS place's printed latitude 41 deg 28.6 min N, longitude 82 deg 11.5 min W. The lighthouse is the tower, so the station point should be the tower.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record dates the first light to 1836 and gives a wooden front range (1836, lost). The library's history describes a cylindrical brick tower built 1837 at the end of the west pier, rebuilt of brick in 1857 and replaced in 1875 by a 46-foot wooden tower. The present concrete tower is a separate structure of 1917-1919; the story treats the earlier lights as the station's predecessors.

Lens and lighting dates: USLHS gives the original fourth-order lens as 1918; the Commissioner's report and the Lighthouse Service Bulletin give the permanent light and fourth-order lens in April 1919 (the USLHS date may be the lens delivery).

The Lorain library's main chronology and the USLHS record give 1966 (last light 10 January 1966). The Ohio historical marker wording in the library gives 1965, and LighthouseFriends says the last crew left in 1965. The story gives 1966 and states the 1965 dating as the marker's and LighthouseFriends'.
The library gives 1837 for the first cylindrical brick tower and 1836 for the appropriation; LighthouseFriends gives 1836 for the tower's construction. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: (1) The library's compilation (2017) is the only source for the 1836-1917 history, the 1888/1894/1912 accidents, the keepers' list before 1919, the Coast Guard years and the restoration. It quotes primary reports, which the story cites directly where the Commissioner and Bulletin texts were read. Its wording is paraphrased; only public-domain report text is quoted. (2) 1894 Alta: the library dates the strike to 16 August 1894 and the fall of the tower to the same time; LighthouseFriends dates the fall to 22 June 1894 and a second strike to 16 August 1895. The story reports the disagreement. (3) First name of the longest-serving keeper: James Connolly (library) vs John Connolly (LighthouseFriends). (4) Roster: USLHS lines are copied as printed. Names from the library's list (pre-1919 heads and assistants, and the 1953-1959 Coast Guard names printed as USCG-1953 etc.) are not checked against NARA. Frank Sellman appears as principal (USLHS, 1919-1921) and first assistant (library list, 1919-1921): both are recorded. Ralph McGue/McGee and Elmer/E.W. Redding are presumed the same men. (5) Status: the record says inactive, deactivated 1965 (Wikidata) or 1966 (USLHS); the library says the Coast Guard's last light was 10 January 1966, and LighthouseFriends says the last crew left in 1965. The record's first_lit 2001 (Wikidata) matches the library's 2001-2002 navigational light in the lantern; the Foundation now says the light is no longer lit. A current Light List check is needed. (6) The record's 'front_range' (wood, 1836, 12.4 m) does not match the library's brick 1837 tower or its 46-foot wooden 1875 tower; left for a human to reconcile. (7) USLHS gives the optic as fourth-order Fresnel installed 1918 and the Commissioner gives 1919. (8) The NRHP nomination (78002108) is not digitised at NPGallery (placeholder); the listing date comes from NPGallery's asset record. (9) Ownership: the library says the Port of Lorain Foundation bought the building in 1990; the Foundation's current legal status and owner of record are not confirmed. (10) Living people: no keepers after 1960 are named except William Deverick's roster line, which the USLHS prints; the 1947-48 Coast Guard memoir in the library is paraphrased without a name. (11) Bulletin OCR is poor in places (e.g. 'tbelr', 'A. Willlams'); the quotes used are the clean OCR strings. (12) Fact-check pass 2026-10-22: removed the unsourced light characteristic 'Fl R 6s' and range 3.4 nm; focal height changed from 9.8 m to 18.3 m (USLHS 'Height of light above mean high water: 60 ft'); the 1922 steel tower replaced the wooden tower at the end of the west pier, not the rear range tower, so the rear range note now says it was discontinued after 1912. Dropped 'climbable': the record does not say the lantern is climbable; the Foundation runs tours (library, 2002 onward). The 1924 Bulletin rescue sentence runs across PDF pages 31-32; the footnote now says so. Fellner is spelled Dawsen in the Bulletin and Dawson in the USLHS roster. The 1966 vs 1965 decommissioning dates and the LighthouseFriends 1836 vs library 1837 tower dates are both in the story text. The check_quotes 'close' quote (Wayne Conn line, a hyphen split across lines in the library PDF) was replaced with a single-line quote.
